title: The Cinnabar Road: Dada, Tradition, and the Flat on the Corso
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Rome, birth on the nineteenth of May
stops.date_confidence: Date and city attested in the English, Italian, German and Spanish Wikipedia articles and in the Treccani Dizionario Biografico. The birth address is recorded nowhere consulted, so the pin is the Rome centroid. The parents' names carry an unresolved split: Italian and Spanish Wikipedia give Vincenzo Evola and Concetta Mangiapane, both of Cinisi in Sicily, while Treccani gives the mother as Concetta Frangipane. The Sicilian form is followed here and the contradiction is not adjudicated.
stops.campa: In a Rome that has been the capital of Italy for less than thirty years, a son is born to Vincenzo Evola and Concetta Mangiapane, both of them out of Cinisi in the province of Palermo, both Catholic. They register him Giulio Cesare Andrea. The household is small-propertied and unremarkable, and nothing in it forecasts a man who will spend fifty years arguing that the modern world is not progress but descent. He will discard nearly everything the house gave him, the Church included, and in time the Italian form of his own first name. The street it stood on is recorded nowhere.
suggested_refs: The Evola and Mangiapane families of Cinisi, province of Palermo
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, the technical school and the refused degree
stops.date_confidence: Attendance at the Istituto Tecnico Leonardo da Vinci and enrolment in engineering are both attested (it.wikipedia; Treccani, which reports that he completed the course without taking the degree). Neither the school years nor the enrolment year is given by any source consulted; 1915 is a placement. The pin is the Via Cavour address of the Leonardo da Vinci institute; the dossier's earlier coordinates fell near the Imperial Fora. The engineering course itself was taught not at the old Sapienza seat but at the Regia Scuola di Applicazione per gli Ingegneri in via Eudossiana, about 200 metres from this pin.
stops.campa: He is sent to the Istituto Tecnico Leonardo da Vinci on Via Cavour, a school for boys headed toward drawing boards rather than toward Greek. The training takes. He keeps a draughtsman's exactness for the rest of his life, and his prose will read like a specification, numbered and sectioned. He goes on to the engineering faculty, two hundred metres away in via Eudossiana, and completes the entire course, then refuses to sit the final examination and refuses the degree. It is the first of the refusals that organize his life: take the training, decline the certificate. He does not want a bourgeois qualification attached to his name.
suggested_refs: The Istituto Tecnico Industriale Leonardo da Vinci, Via Cavour 258, Rome
The Regia Scuola di Applicazione per gli Ingegneri at San Pietro in Vincoli
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, the first canvases and Balla's circle
stops.date_confidence: Treccani dates the first paintings to 1915 and the first poems to 1916; this stop is placed at the later of the two and carries both. The pin is the Rome centroid: no studio address is given in any source consulted.
stops.campa: At seventeen he paints, at eighteen he writes verse. Rome's Futurist milieu is within reach and the circle around Giacomo Balla takes him in: pure color, noise rendered as form, the machine admitted as a subject fit for canvas. The war does not interrupt it. He is an artillery cadet who paints, and who reads Nietzsche and Weininger in the intervals between the two. The canvases of these two years are the first objects he makes that anybody thinks worth keeping. They go into storage in Rome and stay there forty years.
suggested_refs: Guido Andrea Pautasso, Julius Evola: Catalogo ragionato dell'opera artistica (Electa, 20 March 2025), the first analytical catalogue of the paintings, drawings and objects
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Turin, the officers' course
stops.date_confidence: Italian Wikipedia places the artillery officer training at Turin in 1917; the month is not given and is defaulted.
stops.campa: He is sent to Turin for the artillery officers' course. The city is the industrial capital of the country and the army's technical instruction is exact work, arithmetic performed in uniform. He is nineteen. Of the whole apparatus of patriotic feeling arranged around him, the flags, the speeches, the newspapers with their maps, he takes almost nothing; the discipline itself he keeps for the rest of his life. The course is ballistics, ranging tables, and the handling of guns and of the men who serve them, and he is good at it.
suggested_refs: The Royal Artillery school at Turin, 1917 intake

stops.name: Monte Cimone di Tonezza, the mountain battery
stops.date_confidence: Service on Monte Cimone di Tonezza is attested in the English Wikipedia article, which cites a surviving photograph of Evola there in uniform. Month unrecorded. Pin corrected to the Nominatim coordinates for Monte Cimone, Tonezza del Cimone, about a kilometre from the rounded figure the dossier carried.
stops.campa: Posted above the Astico valley to Monte Cimone di Tonezza, he serves in a mountain battery. A photograph survives of him on the mountain in uniform, a thin young officer against rock. The summit he works from is itself a wound: an Austrian mine had taken the top off the Cimone the year before he arrived, killing most of a battalion. He is nineteen, doing what he will later describe as the only thing war reliably offers a man. Not victory, and not the nation. A sustained proximity to being killed.
suggested_refs: The mined summit of Monte Cimone di Tonezza, blown 23 September 1916

stops.name: Asiago plateau, the guns that never fire in anger
stops.date_confidence: The Asiago posting is attested (en.wikipedia; Treccani) for 1917 and 1918; no major action is recorded under Evola's name in any source consulted, and the absence is itself part of the record. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: On the Asiago plateau he holds mountain artillery positions through the last year of the war. Two decades later he will write about war as an ascetic operation, an impersonal ordeal that burns the private person away, and the argument will owe far more to these static months on a plateau than to any battle. Nothing much happens in his sector. There is no engagement recorded under his name, no citation, no wound. He sits with the guns in the cold, on a front that has barely moved since the spring.
stops.quote_source: Julius Evola, Metaphysics of War, English edition 2007, p. 66, via en.wikiquote; written two decades after the war and quoted here for the doctrine, not as testimony from 1918
suggested_refs: The Italian artillery positions on the Asiago plateau, 1917-1918
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Milan, Palazzo Cova and the Futurist exhibition
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Treccani gives April 1919 at Palazzo Cova, Milan, and names the works, one of them in English as Five o'clock tea. The dossier's back-translation Cinque ore del te was an invention and is dropped. The Via Silvio Pellico address for Palazzo Cova is not confirmed by any source reached; the pin is central Milan near the Duomo.
stops.campa: Marinetti's Grande Esposizione Nazionale Futurista opens at Palazzo Cova and Evola hangs among the exhibitors at twenty, showing Fucina, studio di rumori and a canvas whose title he gives in English, Five o'clock tea. Futurism is at its loudest that spring, war-worship and speed and the nation, and he is already restless inside it. He wants the demolition without the flag, and Futurism will not give him one without the other; inside a year he has left it. The catalogue prints his name among the young men of the movement, and prints both titles, one of them in English.
suggested_refs: Julius Evola. Lo spirituale nell'arte, Mart Rovereto, 15 May to 16 October 2022, curated by Beatrice Avanzi and Giorgio Calcara, which returned these canvases to the history of Italian modern art
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, the Casa d'Arte Bragaglia
stops.date_confidence: Attested: a solo exhibition at Anton Giulio Bragaglia's Casa d'Arte in January 1920, with the manifesto Arte astratta: posizione teorica published alongside (en.wikipedia; Treccani). Day unrecorded.
stops.campa: Anton Giulio Bragaglia gives him the Casa d'Arte on Via Condotti for a one-man show, and he publishes a manifesto to go with it, Arte astratta: posizione teorica. The paintings are no longer Futurist. They are abstractions he calls interior landscapes, built to induce a state in the viewer rather than to depict a thing. The theory arriving with them takes its vocabulary from magic rather than from criticism: the picture is described as an operation, and the viewer as the material it is performed on. He is twenty-one.
suggested_refs: Arte astratta: posizione teorica (Rome, 1920)
The Casa d'Arte Bragaglia, Via Condotti
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, the letter to Tristan Tzara
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Treccani, citing the Evola-Tzara correspondence published in 1991 as Lettere di Julius Evola a Tristan Tzara. The founding of Bleu at Mantua with Fiozzi and Cantarelli is attested by Treccani for the same year; whether Evola ever travelled to Mantua or edited entirely by post from Rome is not established anywhere consulted, which is why the review is carried here at his own pin.
stops.campa: He writes to Tristan Tzara and declares himself Dada. Nothing in Italy obliges him to. Dada is a foreign scandal reaching him mainly on paper, and he attaches himself to it by post, in a letter that survives and is printed seventy-one years later. What he wants from it is not the joke. It is the demolition: proof that art, sense and the self can be taken apart deliberately by someone who has chosen to. The same year he founds a Dada review with Aldo Fiozzi and Gino Cantarelli, called Bleu, run out of Mantua, three issues and done. He is already signing himself Julius.
suggested_refs: Lettere di Julius Evola a Tristan Tzara (1991)
Bleu, three issues, Mantua, 1920-1921
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Berlin, sixty canvases at Der Sturm
stops.date_confidence: Attested for January 1921 (Treccani; en.wikipedia), roughly sixty works. Day unrecorded. Pin is the Potsdamer Strasse premises of Der Sturm.
stops.campa: Herwarth Walden takes some sixty of his canvases into Der Sturm on the Potsdamer Strasse, the gallery that has shown Kandinsky, Marc and Chagall. It is the largest exhibition of Evola's work in his lifetime and it happens in Germany rather than Italy, when he is twenty-two. He will keep coming back to Berlin for twenty-five years, on business that has nothing to do with painting. The pictures hang in January on the best avant-garde walls in Europe, and are down again by February.
suggested_refs: The Galerie Der Sturm of Herwarth Walden, Potsdamer Strasse, Berlin
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Paris, the Salon Dada at the Galerie Montaigne
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Treccani independently confirms his participation in the Salon Dada at the Galerie Montaigne, June 1921. The dossier had marked this unverified on an exhausted search budget; the flag was stale. Day unrecorded.
stops.campa: His work hangs in the Salon Dada at the Galerie Montaigne, the movement's set-piece Paris show, among Tzara, Ernst, Ribemont-Dessaignes and the rest. Breton is already pulling in another direction and the Salon stands close to the end of Dada as a shared undertaking. Evola is in Paris for the last days of a thing he had joined by letter eighteen months earlier. What he draws from it is the conclusion the others resist: that a demolition, once carried out, cannot be carried out again. Whether he says so to anyone in the room, nobody records.
suggested_refs: The Salon Dada, Galerie Montaigne, Paris, June 1921
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, the Grotte dell'Augusteo and the painted backdrop
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Treccani for April 1921: Roman Dada evenings at the Grotte dell'Augusteo, with a backdrop painted by Evola. Day unrecorded. Placed before the Paris Salon, which falls in June of the same year.
stops.campa: In the cellars beside the Augusteo the Roman Dadaists hold their evenings, and Evola paints the backdrop they perform in front of. It is as close as Dada in Italy comes to having a stage. He works for a scene he already suspects of being merely a scene, scandal repeated until it hardens into a genre. He does the job anyway, and does it well. The backdrop, like nearly everything painted for a single night, does not survive, and neither do photographs of the room.
suggested_refs: The Grotte dell'Augusteo cabaret, Piazza Augusto Imperatore, Rome
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, the brush laid down
stops.date_confidence: Treccani gives a single year, 1923, for the end of the painting and poetry and the start of what Evola called his philosophical period; the dossier's 1922/1923 range is corrected. The near-suicidal crisis carried in the same campa is tagged R throughout: it rests on Evola's own account in Il cammino del cinabro (1963), with no diary, letter or independent witness known. Treccani reports it as self-report, and the change of name to Julius is dated by Treccani only to this later phase, without a year, while Dada-period works were already signed Julius in 1920.
stops.campa: He stops painting and stops writing verse, and the two things he has done since he was seventeen simply end. In his telling the avant-garde was a road that had to be walked to its end so that the end could be seen, and he turns from it to philosophy. Somewhere just before, on his own account given forty years later, he comes to the edge of killing himself. No diary, no letter and no witness confirms it. What he says stopped him is a line out of an early Buddhist text: whoever takes extinction as an object of craving has extinguished nothing.
suggested_refs: Il cammino del cinabro (1963), the sole source for the crisis of c. 1922
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

segments.name: Magical Idealism and the Group of Ur

stops.name: Rome, magical idealism and the theosophists' hall
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Atanor of Rome published Saggi sull'idealismo magico and L'uomo come potenza in 1925 (Treccani). The lectures are attested for 1925 by Treccani, at the Independent Theosophical League of Rome presided over by Decio Calvari, editor of Ultra, for which Evola had written since 1923; the dossier's unverified flag was stale. Month unrecorded. The quote is tagged R: it is given in the English Wikipedia article, footnote 71, attributed to this 1925 work, and neither the Italian original nor a full translation was seen.
stops.campa: Atanor publishes Saggi sull'idealismo magico, and the same year L'uomo come potenza. The argument is that the absolute I is not a given but a task: the self must become the source of its own reality, and philosophy is worth nothing unless it issues in operations that change whoever performs them. German idealism, pushed until it turns into a manual. Meanwhile Decio Calvari, who edits the neo-spiritualist review Ultra and heads the Independent Theosophical League, lends him the League's rooms for a course of lectures. He has been writing for Ultra since 1923, and he is teaching inside the milieu he is preparing to take apart.
stops.quote: God does not exist. The Ego must create him by making itself divine.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Saggi sull'idealismo magico (1925) in en.wikipedia, 'Julius Evola', footnote 71; the Italian original was not seen and the wording is unverified
suggested_refs: Saggi sull'idealismo magico (Atanor, Rome, 1925)
The review Ultra of Decio Calvari and the Independent Theosophical League of Rome
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, Sibilla Aleramo and the first political article
stops.date_confidence: The relationship with Sibilla Aleramo is attested by Italian Wikipedia, which cites her own 1927 novel Amo dunque sono; the twenty-two year gap checks against her birth in 1876 and his in 1898. The character name Tellegra, carried by the dossier, appears in no source reached and is dropped. Treccani's Evola entry does not mention Aleramo at all, so the dossier's source attribution for this item was wrong. The article Stato, potenza, liberta in Lo Stato democratico is separately attested by Treccani to 1 May 1925.
stops.campa: Sibilla Aleramo, born Rina Faccio, forty-nine years old and the most famous woman writer in Italy, takes up with a man of twenty-seven who has just published a book about becoming God. The affair is stormy and she writes it down; her novel Amo dunque sono puts him on the page as she found him, doctrinal and unreachable. He is not yet attached to anything. His first openly political article had appeared in a liberal anti-regime paper of all places, Duke Giovanni Colonna di Cesaro's Lo Stato democratico, on the first of May 1925.
suggested_refs: Sibilla Aleramo, Amo dunque sono (1927)
Stato, potenza, liberta, in Lo Stato democratico, 1 May 1925
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, the Gruppo di Ur
stops.date_confidence: Treccani dates the gathering of the circle around Arturo Reghini to the end of 1926, which the English Wikipedia article's 1926 founding date supports; the dossier's 1927 is corrected. The journals are firmly dated: Ur monthly through 1927-1928, continued as Krur in 1929. Day defaulted. The stop is placed in date order, before the Guenon stop of 1927.
stops.campa: A small circle gathers around Arturo Reghini: Evola, Giovanni Colazza, a dozen others, most of them writing under Latin pseudonyms. They call it Ur and they do not treat it as a reading group. The monthly issues, running two years and continued as Krur, print instructions rather than essays: breathing, visualization, the handling of states of consciousness, Hermetic and Tantric and early Buddhist material laid out as procedure to be performed. The group works for three years and then breaks apart, over Evola's politics and over Reghini's Masonry.
suggested_refs: Ur, monthly, 1927-1928, and Krur, 1929, collected as Introduzione alla magia quale scienza dell'Io
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, the master he will not obey
stops.date_confidence: The influence is attested: English Wikipedia states that Guenon's La Crise du monde moderne, published in Paris in 1927, moved Evola to organise his thought around a critique of modernity, and that he called Guenon his master while diverging from him. The correspondence and the argument over Vedanta are attested from the mid-1920s; Reghini as the Roman channel is reported in the dossier and is not independently confirmed here. The year is the publication year of the Guenon book, used to place the stop; the month is defaulted.
stops.campa: Rene Guenon's La Crise du monde moderne reaches him through the Roman esoteric circles and reorganizes everything he has. From Guenon he takes the whole apparatus: the cycles, the Kali Yuga, a Tradition that is single and prior to all religions, modernity read as descent rather than as progress. He calls Guenon his master. He also disagrees with him, almost at once, about the only question that matters between them: whether the highest human type is the contemplative priest or the acting king. Evola chooses the king. They argue it by letter for the next thirty years and neither of them concedes.
suggested_refs: Rene Guenon, La Crise du monde moderne (Paris, 1927)
The Evola-Guenon correspondence held by the Fondazione Julius Evola, Rome

stops.name: Rome, Imperialismo pagano
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Treccani for 1928, a year before the Lateran Pacts of February 1929. Month unrecorded.
stops.campa: He publishes Imperialismo pagano and attacks the Church head-on, at full length and under his own name. The book tells Fascism to its face that Christianity is the European disease, and that any real empire would have to be pagan, Roman, solar and hierarchical, built on caste and on rite. It is close to the worst argument a man can make in Italy in 1928, and he addresses it to the regime rather than to the faithful. Fourteen months later Mussolini signs the Lateran Pacts and settles sixty years of quarrel between the Italian state and the Vatican.
suggested_refs: Imperialismo pagano: il fascismo dinanzi al pericolo euro-cristiano (1928)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, La Torre and the intervention of Starace
stops.date_confidence: Attested: ten issues from February to June 1930 (Treccani; it.wikipedia), and Treccani states that criticism in its pages provoked the intervention of party secretary Achille Starace. The printers' boycott as a mechanism is a shade more specific than the sources state. The quote is verified from the facsimile of Evola's formal notice reproduced in the Italian edition of Il cammino del cinabro; note that it is first person plural, written for the journal, and that it belongs to 1930 and not, as Wikipedia's compression of Cassina Wolff has it, to the 1951 trial.
stops.campa: He founds La Torre, a fortnightly, and uses it to attack the regime from the right: its demographic campaign, its populism, its appetite for conformists, its confusion of a crowd with a nation. Ten issues appear between February and June. Achille Starace, the party secretary, intervenes; printers stop taking the work and distribution is obstructed, and the paper closes. Answering a charge of anti-Fascism in his own pages, Evola does not deny the regime and does not defend himself. He outbids it.
stops.quote: E FANTASTICA L'ACCUSA DI ANTIFASCISMO, SE MAI SIAMO SUPERFASCISTI
stops.quote_source: Formal notice printed in La Torre, 1930, facsimile reproduced in the Italian edition of Il cammino del cinabro; corroborated by editorial matter in Men Among the Ruins and by Marco Tarchi, 'La Torre o il tentativo superfascista'
suggested_refs: La Torre, ten issues, February to June 1930
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: The Dolomites, the school of the peaks
stops.date_confidence: Tagged R throughout. That Evola climbed and wrote about climbing is not in doubt, and the essays were gathered posthumously as Meditazioni delle vette, but no specific peak, route or date is established in any source consulted, and claims of a major first ascent are unsubstantiated. The pin near Cortina d'Ampezzo is an illustrative Dolomites marker, not a claim about where he climbed.
stops.campa: Through the years when he is least visible politically, he climbs. The high mountain in his essays is neither sport nor scenery. It is a place where the personal element is burned off by cold and exposure and the standing possibility of a fall, leaving what he calls the solar state, an impersonal clarity available nowhere lower down. The pieces are collected long after his death as Meditazioni delle vette. Not one route, summit or ascent of his has ever been documented by anybody except himself.
suggested_refs: Meditazioni delle vette, collected posthumously from the alpine essays

stops.name: Rome, the hermetic tradition as an operative art
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Treccani for 1931, published by Laterza at Bari, not at Rome as the dossier had it; the pin is Evola's own city, since he wrote in Rome and no evidence places him at the publisher. The incognito stays in Carthusian, Carmelite and old-rule Benedictine houses, carried in the same campa, are tagged R: neither a specific house nor a date is established anywhere consulted.
stops.campa: Laterza of Bari publishes La tradizione ermetica, and the alchemists come out of the history of chemistry. Evola reads the entire corpus as operative: furnace, black work, mercury and sulphur are a notation for transformations performed on the operator, and the gold was never metal. It is the most controlled book he has written and the one least interested in politics; for two hundred pages the modern world goes unmentioned. In these same years, briefly and without giving his name, he asks to be taken in at Carthusian, Carmelite and old-rule Benedictine houses, to watch a discipline work from inside it.
suggested_refs: La tradizione ermetica (Laterza, Bari, 1931)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'
Dossier assertion for the monastery stays, not independently confirmed

stops.name: Rome, the mask and the face of the spiritualists
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Treccani for 1932, published by Bocca at Turin, not at Rome as the dossier had it; pinned at Rome for the same reason as the preceding stop. Month unrecorded.
stops.campa: Bocca of Turin publishes Maschera e volto dello spiritualismo contemporaneo, and he turns on his own neighbours. The halls he has lectured in for seven years are theosophical halls, and the book costs him them. Theosophy, spiritualism, the seance, Steiner's anthroposophy and Freudian psychoanalysis are taken up one at a time and dismissed as counterfeits: subpersonal states mistaken for superpersonal ones, mediums confusing passivity with attainment, the unconscious mistaken for a depth when it is only a basement.
suggested_refs: Maschera e volto dello spiritualismo contemporaneo (Bocca, Turin, 1932)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

segments.name: The Doctrine of Race and the Two Regimes

stops.name: Milan, Rivolta contro il mondo moderno
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 1934, published by Hoepli of Milan (Treccani; en.wikipedia); month unrecorded. Pinned at the Milan publisher since no evidence places the writing anywhere but Rome and the book's public existence begins here. The quote is verified against the Stucco translation, chapter on the regression of the castes, at approximately p. 327; the dossier's wording, 'The social bond assumes a utilitarian and economic character', appears nowhere in Evola and its citation to Men Among the Ruins p. 34 is false, the string 'social bond' occurring zero times in that translation.
stops.campa: Hoepli publishes Rivolta contro il mondo moderno, and everything he writes afterward is a defence of it. Two parts. First the world of Tradition, reconstructed as a single order of caste, sacred kingship, rite and centre; then the genesis of the modern world, told as a fall through four ages ending in the one now running. Nothing in it is argued the way a historian argues, and the case does not rest on evidence at all. It rests on a claim to see a form that the evidence, by its nature, cannot show. He is thirty-six when it appears.
stops.quote: At this time the social bond was no longer a fides of a warrior type based on relationships of faithfulness and honor. Instead, it took on a utilitarian and economic character; it consisted of an agreement based on personal convenience and on material interest that only a merchant could have conceived.
stops.quote_source: Julius Evola, Revolt Against the Modern World, trans. Guido Stucco (Inner Traditions, 1995), chapter on the regression of the castes, p. approx. 327
suggested_refs: Rivolta contro il mondo moderno (Hoepli, Milan, 1934)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Cremona, the Diorama filosofico in Farinacci's paper
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day at both ends by Treccani: the Diorama filosofico ran in Il Regime fascista from 2 February 1934 to 18 July 1943. The paper was Cremona-based; Evola edited the page from Rome.
stops.campa: Roberto Farinacci, the most brutal of the provincial Fascist bosses, hands him a page. From the second of February the Diorama filosofico appears inside Il Regime fascista out of Cremona, and Evola edits it in the newspaper of the party's hardest wing, printing Rene Guenon, Coomaraswamy, the German conservatives and his own reviews. It is the strangest arrangement of his life, an anti-modern metaphysician carried on the budget of a squadrista, and the longest platform he ever holds: nine years and five months, ending with the issue of 18 July 1943, a week before Mussolini falls.
suggested_refs: The Diorama filosofico page in Il Regime fascista, 2 February 1934 to 18 July 1943
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Berlin and Bremen, the Herrenklub tour
stops.date_confidence: The 1934 German lecture activity is corroborated by Italian Wikipedia and centrostudilaruna; Treccani names Berlin and Bremen. The Deutscher Herrenklub venue specifically and the Rohan connection are dossier claims not independently confirmed here. Month unrecorded and defaulted; the tour is placed after the Cremona page for narrative order only, and may have fallen later in the year. Bremen, at 53.0793, 8.8017, is carried in this campa rather than given a pin of its own, since nothing is preserved of what he said there.
stops.campa: He lectures in Berlin and moves in the Deutscher Herrenklub, the aristocratic-conservative circle around Prince Karl Anton Rohan where the German Conservative Revolution keeps its address book. These are men of the old right who despise the Nazis as plebeian and who will mostly be broken by them within five years. Evola tells them he prefers them to the party, in Germany, in the year Hitler completes his hold on the state. He speaks at Bremen on the same tour. Of that lecture nothing survives at all: a city, a year, and no text attached to either.
suggested_refs: The Deutscher Herrenklub, Berlin, and the circle of Prince Karl Anton Rohan
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, the Jewish question and the forgery
stops.date_confidence: Tre aspetti del problema ebraico, Rome 1936, is confirmed in Treccani's bibliography. The 1937 edition of the Protocols with Evola's introduction is NOT in the Treccani entry, so the dossier's source attribution for that half was wrong; it is separately well attested that he prefaced the edition issued through Giovanni Preziosi's La Vita Italiana, and that attestation needs its own citation, which this pass did not obtain. The two publications are carried in one stop with the second tagged R on its sourcing.
stops.campa: He publishes Tre aspetti del problema ebraico and enters the argument he never gets out of. His position is that the Jewish question is spiritual rather than biological, which he offers as a refinement and which works as a licence: it lets him hold German racial biology at arm's length while supplying Italian antisemitism with a metaphysics. The following year an Italian edition of the Protocols of the Elders of Zion appears with an introduction by him. The document had been proved a forgery in London in 1921, and he knows it, and he writes that the question of authenticity is beside the point.
suggested_refs: Tre aspetti del problema ebraico (Rome, 1936)
The 1937 Italian Protocols edition issued through Giovanni Preziosi's La Vita Italiana
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'
Dossier assertion for the 1937 Protocols introduction, source attribution corrected, own citation not obtained

stops.name: Romania, at Codreanu's house
stops.date_confidence: Italian Wikipedia is explicit: in March 1938 Evola met Corneliu Codreanu in Romania, at Codreanu's own residence. The dossier's 1937 is corrected; the difference matters, since March 1938 places the meeting months rather than a year before Codreanu's killing. Treccani names Codreanu only in a list of European right-wing contacts, alongside Mircea Eliade, and describes no Romanian journey, so Treccani cannot carry this. The Bucharest pin is an approximation: the source places the meeting at a residence, not in the city generically. The essay La tragedia della Guardia di Ferro is dated 1938 by Treccani without a month and is tagged R. The quote is verified verbatim in the Stucco translation but Evola is there listing traditional sayings, not speaking in his own voice.
stops.campa: He travels to Romania and is received at Corneliu Zelea Codreanu's own house. What he takes away is a portrait of the Legion's captain as an ascetic: the fasting, the prison years, a religious rather than a political style, everything Evola believes a movement of the right should be and Italian Fascism is not. He is moving in the same Bucharest intellectual world as Mircea Eliade, whom he knows and corresponds with. Codreanu is strangled by gendarmes before the year is out, the killing reported as an escape attempt, and Evola answers with an essay on the tragedy of the Iron Guard.
stops.quote: The blood of the heroes is closer to God than the ink of the philosophers and the prayers of the faithful.
stops.quote_source: Quoted by Evola in Revolt Against the Modern World, trans. Guido Stucco (Inner Traditions, 1995), chapter 'The Greater and the Lesser Holy War', p. approx. 125, where he cites it in quotation marks as a traditional warrior saying alongside 'Paradise lies under the shade of the swords'; it is not his own aphorism and Wikiquote's presentation of it as such is a misattribution
suggested_refs: La tragedia della Guardia di Ferro (1938)
The Legion of the Archangel Michael and the November 1938 killings
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Florence and Milan, the lectures on race
stops.date_confidence: The lecture cycle is attested by Italian Wikipedia, which names both universities and Giuseppe Bottai as the minister who requested it, but says only 'in those years' and gives no date; the year 1939 is therefore tagged R, and so is the dossier's reported 1939 offer of a chair of racism at Rome, which appears in no source reached. Milan, at 45.4622, 9.1946, is carried in this campa rather than pinned separately.
stops.campa: Giuseppe Bottai, Minister of National Education, arranges a cycle of lectures for him at the universities of Florence and Milan on the doctrine of race. Italy passed its racial laws the year before and needs a theory to stand behind them. Evola has one ready and it is not the German one: race as a matter of body, soul and spirit together, with the spirit deciding, so that a man may be of the wrong blood and the right type or the reverse. It earns him enemies in both directions, too mystical for the anthropologists and too German for the Church. He never receives a chair.
suggested_refs: The Italian racial laws of 1938 and the university lecture cycle requested by Bottai
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Palazzo Venezia, the audience with Mussolini
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Treccani confirms he was summoned in September 1941, and centrostudilaruna states the meeting took place at Palazzo Venezia; the dossier's hedge that the venue was merely inferred from Mussolini's known office was too cautious. Sintesi di dottrina della razza, Hoepli, Milan, 1941, is attested by Treccani and en.wikipedia. Day unrecorded.
stops.campa: Hoepli publishes Sintesi di dottrina della razza, and in September Mussolini has him brought to Palazzo Venezia. The Duce has read the book and likes it: here at last is a racial doctrine that is Italian, hierarchical and not borrowed from Berlin. He backs the proposal of a joint Italian-German review to carry it. Nothing comes of the proposal, and Evola is given no post and no institute. This is the highest his access to power ever reaches: one audience, at the far end of a very long room.
suggested_refs: Sintesi di dottrina della razza (Hoepli, Milan, 1941)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Berlin, the review that never appears
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Treccani for February 1942: travel to Germany seeking backing for the proposed Italian-German racial journal, which never appeared amid bureaucratic opposition. Day unrecorded; the Berlin pin is the standard city centroid, no address being given.
stops.campa: He goes to Germany to find backing for the review Mussolini approved. The German racial bureaucracy has no use for an Italian metaphysician who thinks its biology is vulgar, and the offices he needs are held by men whose careers rest on that biology. He keeps the appointments through February and nothing is signed. The review never appears. He is forty-three, and this is as far out as his influence reaches: one head of government's approval, and a run of meetings in Berlin offices that lead nowhere.
suggested_refs: The unrealised Italian-German racial review of 1941-1942
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

segments.name: The German Years and the Spine

stops.name: Berlin, named to the Germans by Preziosi
stops.date_confidence: Treccani supports this directly: after 25 July it was again Preziosi who pointed Evola out to the Germans. Late August is the dossier's placement; the month is not given by Treccani and the day is defaulted.
stops.campa: Mussolini falls on the twenty-fifth of July and Rome becomes, overnight, a dangerous city for a man with Evola's bibliography. Giovanni Preziosi, the country's most committed antisemite, names him to the Germans, and he is flown north. Everything he does from here to the end of the war he does inside the German apparatus. The work proposed to him is a study of Jewish and Masonic influence inside the Italian establishment that has just collapsed: an autopsy of the regime performed for the benefit of its ally. He accepts.
suggested_refs: Giovanni Preziosi and the review La Vita Italiana
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Munich, among the Italians who chose Germany
stops.date_confidence: Italian Wikipedia places him in Munich after 8 September 1943; the date is the armistice, used to order the segment, not a record of his arrival. His judgement of the Salo republic as republican and socializing is reported rather than quoted here.
stops.campa: After the armistice of the eighth of September he is in Munich, inside the improvised world of Italians who have chosen Germany over the king: Fascists flown out of the country, officials in transit, a new republic being assembled in hotel rooms and requisitioned offices. Evola is present for the assembling and takes no post in it. He thinks Salo is a mistake, a republican and socializing Fascism, the last thing he had wanted from any of it. What he wants is a legitimist restoration, and nobody in those hotel rooms is proposing one.
suggested_refs: The founding of the Italian Social Republic, September 1943

stops.name: Rastenburg, the Wolf's Lair he says he stood in
stops.date_confidence: Tagged R, and the most over-tagged claim in the dossier. The Rastenburg presence appears in none of Treccani, English, German or Italian Wikipedia; English Wikipedia says only that Evola fled to Nazi Germany in 1943 and returned to Rome under the Italian Social Republic. The claim traces to Evola's own account in Il cammino del cinabro. The sole source the dossier cited, centrostudilaruna, dates his presence to 8 September 1943, four days before Mussolini's rescue from the Gran Sasso, and so cannot describe a party receiving the rescued Duce. The date here is Mussolini's rescue, used only to order the segment. The quote is from a book written twenty-seven years later.
stops.campa: By his own account, given twenty years afterward, he is at the Wolf's Lair in the days around Mussolini's rescue from the Gran Sasso, standing in the party that receives the freed Duce at the forest headquarters in East Prussia. No document places him there. No photograph, no list, no German or Italian record confirms it, and the one source that dates his presence puts it four days before the rescue it claims he witnessed. It is the most famous scene of his war and the least attested, and the only witness who ever describes it is Evola.
stops.quote: Prussia had been the creation of a dynasty that had the nobility, the army and the higher bureaucracy for its backbone.
stops.quote_source: Julius Evola, Notes on the Third Reich (1970), p. 37, via en.wikiquote; written a quarter-century after the events of this stop
suggested_refs: Il cammino del cinabro (1963), the sole source for the Rastenburg presence
sources: Evola's self-report via Il cammino del cinabro
centrostudilaruna.it, 'Biografia di Julius Evola', whose dating is internally incoherent

stops.name: Vienna, the seized archives
stops.date_confidence: Treccani attests the Vienna work on material seized from Masonic and Jewish organisations, citing Cospito and Neulen, eds., Julius Evola nei documenti segreti del Terzo Reich (1986); the dossier's flag of this as unconfirmed was stale. The nature of his status is genuinely disputed among historians and is left unresolved here. Month unrecorded. Also carried at this pin, and dropped as a separate stop for want of any documentation: the attempted Movimento per la Rinascita dell'Italia in German-occupied Rome, for which no membership, paper or statute has been found.
stops.campa: In Vienna he works on Masonic and Jewish material seized across occupied Europe and brought into the ideological research offices of the SS. What exactly he is doing there is disputed, and the dispute cannot be settled from what survives: a scholar granted access to captured archives, or a man carried on the books of an intelligence service that is at this moment feeding the machinery of extermination. Both readings have historians behind them. He is in the building either way, in 1944, with the confiscated papers open in front of him.
suggested_refs: Cospito and Neulen, eds., Julius Evola nei documenti segreti del Terzo Reich (1986)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Vienna, the fragment and the spine
stops.date_confidence: Spring 1945, month contested: Treccani says April 1945, Italian Wikipedia says March. The projectile is contested too, German Wikipedia saying a Soviet air raid, English a Soviet shell fragment, Spanish a shell fragment, Treccani only a bombardment. Treccani does confirm the striking detail that he deliberately refused to go down to the shelters. No source identifies the street; the pin is the Vienna centroid. The two years in Austrian clinics, ending with the 1948 return, are carried in this campa: Treccani gives two years, and the dossier's 1945-1948 range overstated it by one.
stops.campa: The bombardment of Vienna is nearly continuous now and he will not go down into the shelters. He walks in it deliberately, treating the raids as a test of a doctrine about danger he has been writing for fifteen years. In the spring a fragment reaches his spine. He is forty-six, and he will not walk again. Two years follow in Austrian hospitals and clinics, the paralysis complete below the waist and permanent, and he refuses then and afterward to call it a misfortune: he had put a question, he says, and this is the answer. He never described the moment itself.
suggested_refs: The Vienna raids of March and April 1945
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Bologna, carried back into Italy
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Treccani gives the 1948 return after two years in Austrian clinics, and centrostudilaruna has him hospitalised at Bologna. Month unrecorded.
stops.campa: He is brought back into Italy in 1948 and stops first at Bologna, in hospital again. Everything he had is gone: the page in Cremona, the audience, the regime, the German connection, the use of his legs. He is fifty years old. He has a dozen published books that no respectable Italian house will now touch, and the political tradition he belongs to has just lost a world war and been written out of the constitution. The second half of his working life begins from this bed. He has twenty-six years left and will spend nearly all of them in one room.
suggested_refs: The Bologna hospital stay of 1948
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, arrested with the FAR
stops.date_confidence: Attested for May 1951 by Treccani and centrostudilaruna: arrested with defendants associated with the Fasci di Azione Rivoluzionaria, roughly a month in custody. Day unrecorded; the pin is central Rome, no place of arrest being specified.
stops.campa: The police take him in with the young men of the Fasci di Azione Rivoluzionaria, charged with attempting to reconstitute the dissolved Fascist party and with being the doctrinal head of a clandestine group. He spends about a month in custody. He has held no office, joined no party and given no order to anybody. What the prosecution has is a shelf of his books and a set of defendants half his age who had read them. He is fifty-two years old and he cannot walk.
suggested_refs: The Fasci di Azione Rivoluzionaria prosecution, Rome, 1951
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Piazza Cavour, the self-defence and the acquittal
stops.date_confidence: The date is confirmed by Italian Wikipedia, which gives the trial's conclusion as 20 November 1951, and the outcome by Treccani: twenty-three of thirty-six defendants acquitted, thirteen sentenced. The courthouse identification is inferential. Pin corrected to the Nominatim coordinates for the Palazzo di Giustizia; the dossier's longitude fell in the Tiber. The quote comes from Evola's Autodifesa in Joscelyn Godwin's translation, printed as an appendix to Men Among the Ruins (Inner Traditions, 2002), read in full for this pass: it contains no occurrence of superfascista, contrary to the English Wikipedia compression of Cassina Wolff 2016, and that word belongs to La Torre in 1930.
stops.campa: He is carried into the courtroom on a stretcher and conducts his own defence. He refuses both of the roles the court has available. Not a victim of Fascism, and not an anti-Fascist; and not a Fascist either, since the ideas he holds are older than the movement and will outlast it. If holding them is criminal, he tells the bench, then Aristotle, Plato, the Dante of the De Monarchia and on down to Metternich and Bismarck should be sitting beside him in the dock. Twenty-three of the thirty-six defendants are acquitted. He is one of them.
stops.quote: I do not intend to present myself either as an antifascist or as a victim of Fascism.
stops.quote_source: Julius Evola, Autodifesa, Rome, 1951, trans. Joscelyn Godwin, printed as an appendix to Men Among the Ruins (Inner Traditions, 2002)
suggested_refs: The Autodifesa of 1951, printed in full in the Inner Traditions edition of Men Among the Ruins
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Corso Vittorio Emanuele, the room he does not leave
stops.date_confidence: The street is attested by Italian Wikipedia, which gives no number; the house number 197 carried by the dossier could not be verified in any source reached and is tagged R. The date is corrected from the dossier's 1948: centrostudilaruna gives his permanent Rome residence only from the end of 1951, which fits the Austrian convalescence, the Bologna stay and the May arrest. The pin falls on Corso Vittorio Emanuele II and is a street-level marker, not a building identification.
stops.campa: He settles at last into a flat on the Corso Vittorio Emanuele, and from here he will hardly move again for twenty-three years. Most of his influence is exercised from this room. Visitors climb the stairs by appointment: students, veterans of a lost war, young men out of the neo-Fascist parties, occultists, editors, the occasional foreign writer who has tracked down the address. He receives them from a wheelchair at a desk by the window, gives each of them half an hour, and sends them away with a reading list.
suggested_refs: The flat on Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, Rome, house number unverified

stops.name: Rome, Gli uomini e le rovine
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Treccani for 1953, with an introduction by Prince Junio Valerio Borghese in the original edition. Month unrecorded.
stops.campa: Gli uomini e le rovine appears with a preface by Prince Junio Valerio Borghese, commander of the Decima Mas, whose own death sentence had been commuted six years earlier. The book is addressed to men who have lost: how to hold a position with no state behind it, what an apolitical elite owes to a ruined country, why the party system is the ruin and not the repair. Most of the men who read it never meet him, and he would mostly not have received them. For the next thirty years it is the handbook of the Italian radical right.
suggested_refs: Gli uomini e le rovine (1953), preface by Junio Valerio Borghese
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, Cavalcare la tigre
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Treccani for 1961, Milan publisher; the writing is placed at the flat. Month unrecorded. The quote is reported from en.wikiquote with the citation given there and was not cross-checked against a scan.
stops.campa: Cavalcare la tigre goes further and removes the last consolation. No restoration is coming. The age has to be ridden until it exhausts itself, and what remains available to the differentiated man is apoliteia: an inner detachment that engages the modern world completely and is untouched by any of it, together with a set of disciplines for living inside a dissolution without dissolving. Of everything he wrote it is the book that travels furthest. He writes it at sixty-three, paralysed, in one room off a Roman street, with the traffic of the Corso going past below.
stops.quote: In a large city, in mass society, among the almost unreal swarming of faceless beings, an essential sense of isolation or of detachment often occurs naturally
stops.quote_source: Julius Evola, Ride the Tiger (1961), English edition 2003, p. 121, via en.wikiquote
suggested_refs: Cavalcare la tigre (1961)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Rome, the cinnabar road and the pictures sold
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Treccani for 1963: Il cammino del cinabro, and a Rome retrospective at the Galleria La Medusa the same year which reportedly sold every exhibited work. The word reportedly is Treccani's own hedge and is kept. Month unrecorded. The pin is the Galleria La Medusa rather than the flat, since that is where the exhibition stood.
stops.campa: He publishes Il cammino del cinabro, an intellectual autobiography built as an alchemical work, black then white then red, with his own books arranged as stages of one continuous operation running from the Dada canvases to Cavalcare la tigre. It is retrospective construction and he does not pretend otherwise; the point is to show that a life had a form. The war years are handled briefly, the Vienna archives in a paragraph. The same year the Galleria La Medusa hangs the paintings of 1918 to 1922, out of storage after forty years, and reportedly every one of them sells.
suggested_refs: Il cammino del cinabro (1963)
The 1963 retrospective at the Galleria La Medusa, Rome
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Corso Vittorio Emanuele, Miguel Serrano at the door
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Serrano's own chronology, 1970 entry, quoted here verbatim. Treccani's Evola entry does not mention Serrano at all, so the dossier's source attribution was wrong. Month unrecorded. The 1992 publication date of El secreto de Julius Evola could not be verified from any source reached and is tagged R; the elaborated version of the meeting belongs to Serrano's later literary retellings, not to this chronology line.
stops.campa: Miguel Serrano, Chilean diplomat and writer, having looked for Ezra Pound in Venice and failed to find him, comes on to Rome and the flat on the Corso Vittorio Emanuele. His own chronology records the visit in a single line and says nothing whatever about what passed between them. The elaborate version, the dying master handing over a final secret, belongs to books Serrano writes much later. Evola is seventy-two. He receives Serrano as he receives everyone, at the desk by the window, and leaves no account of the meeting at all.
stops.quote: Busca sin exito en Venecia al escritor americano Ezra Pound y en Roma visita a Julius Evola, pensador tradicionalista italiano.
stops.quote_source: Miguel Serrano's own chronology, 1970 entry, miguelserrano.cl
suggested_refs: Miguel Serrano, El secreto de Julius Evola, the later and far more elaborate retelling

stops.name: Rome, death at the window
stops.date_confidence: Death date and place attested by Treccani and en.wikipedia; the cause, cardiac failure, is given by Spanish Wikipedia. Age 76 checks against 19 May 1898. The posture at death, brought upright to face the Janiculum, is tagged R: it is follower testimony recorded afterward, and the dossier itself flags that it should be attributed to witnesses rather than presented as certified.
stops.campa: He dies in the flat on the eleventh of June, three weeks past his seventy-sixth birthday, of heart failure. Those who were in the room say he asked to be brought upright at the window, facing the Janiculum, and died sitting. They are followers writing afterward and they are the only source there is for the posture. He had been unable to stand for twenty-nine years. He leaves no tomb: the will specifies cremation, and it specifies where the ashes are to be taken.
suggested_refs: The Fondazione Julius Evola, Rome, custodian of the archive and correspondence
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'

stops.name: Monte Rosa, the ashes and no grave
stops.date_confidence: Monte Rosa is attested by both Treccani and Italian Wikipedia and they disagree about what was done: Treccani says the ashes were buried on Monte Rosa, Italian Wikipedia says they were scattered on the summits. The crevasse, the month of August, and the two names carried by the dossier, Renato Del Ponte and the guide Eugene David, appear in neither and are tagged R. The August date is used only to place the stop after the June death. The pin lies within about 300 metres of the Dufourspitze.
stops.campa: The ashes go up onto Monte Rosa. Two men are said to have carried the urn onto the massif and left it in the ice, and the accounts of what they did there do not agree: buried, in one telling; scattered on the summits, in another; dropped into a crevasse, in the version his followers prefer. Two names are attached to the carrying in the retellings, and neither appears in any source that can be checked. The mountain he had written about as a school of impersonal detachment is the only address he now has. There is no grave, no stone and no place anyone can visit, and that was the instruction.
suggested_refs: The Monte Rosa massif on the Italian-Swiss frontier, disposition of the ashes, summer 1974
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giulio Cesare Andrea Evola'
